prompt.context: Our client is a pharmaceutical manufacturer that has just released a new drug 18 months ago and has been underwhelmed with sales. They want BCG to figure out why the sales have been so dismal, and also, what can be done about it.
prompt.question: Why have sales of the client's new drug been so dismal, and what can be done to increase sales?

clarifying_info.q: What competitive landscape does the drug operate in?
clarifying_info.a: There are many kinds of drugs that treat hypertension grouped into 5 classes. Our drug is in a new class — class six.

clarifying_info.q: What is the pricing of the drug?
clarifying_info.a: Our drug retails for $120 a month; after insurance covers a portion, patients pay $25 a month out of pocket.

All other classes but one have gone generic and retail at $4 a month after insurance. The one non-generic class is ARP, which also retails at $120 a month with a similar insurance breakdown. However, half of ARP drugs will have patents expire next year and the other half in two years, so all ARP drugs will go generic within two years.

clarifying_info.q: How effective is the drug compared to competitors?
clarifying_info.a: Our drug lowers blood pressure by about 14 mmHg. The range across all drugs is 14–17 mmHg; ARP drugs lower blood pressure to around 14–16 mmHg. So our drug is on the low end. Doctors prefer drugs that lower pressure as much as possible, though hypotension is also a concern.

clarifying_info.q: Does the drug have any side effects or drug interactions?
clarifying_info.a: The drug is safe with no reactions to other drugs and no side effects.

clarifying_info.q: What is the key differentiator for our drug?
clarifying_info.a: Our drug stays in the system longer. With standard hypertension medication, missing a once-daily dose causes blood pressure to spike even higher than before starting the drug — very unsafe. With our drug, missing a dose causes no problem.

clarifying_info.q: What is the relationship with insurance companies?
clarifying_info.a: The drug company has good relations with most insurance carriers and the drug has gotten onto most formularies and is easily accessible. Contacting insurance companies has been exhausted and there is marketing saturation with the company's means of reaching other insurers — pushing to more insurance companies is not an option.

clarifying_info.q: What do patients know about the drug?
clarifying_info.a: Patients don't know much about blood pressure drugs and don't really care what they get.

clarifying_info.q: What do doctors know about the drug?
clarifying_info.a: Doctors are aware of the drug but think it is very expensive, do not believe it is on formularies, and are not sure when and to whom to prescribe it.

framework: Competitive landscape and product differentiation — understand the drug's class, pricing, efficacy, and unique value proposition relative to competitors
Stakeholder analysis — map which players (insurers, doctors, patients) influence prescribing and purchasing decisions and identify gaps in each
Root cause of low sales — diagnose whether the problem is access/formulary, pricing/cost perception, physician awareness/education, or patient demand
Marketing and action plan — develop targeted initiatives for each stakeholder group to address identified gaps
Recommendation — prioritize highest-impact levers and outline next steps

questions.prompt: Phase 1: Assess the competitive landscape. What are the key competitive dynamics and how does our drug compare?
questions.guidance: Strong answers should identify: (1) 4 of 5 existing drug classes have gone generic at $4/month — a very low price point creating a high bar on cost. (2) The only remaining branded competitor is ARP at $120/month but ARP will be fully generic within 2 years, eliminating price parity competition over time. (3) Our drug is in a new class (class 6) with a moderate efficacy profile (14 mmHg — low end of 14–17 range) but a unique safety differentiator: missing a dose does not cause dangerous blood pressure spikes. (4) Doctors prefer drugs that lower blood pressure more, but the miss-a-dose safety feature is a meaningful clinical differentiator for certain patient segments (e.g., non-adherent patients).

questions.prompt: Phase 2: Stakeholder analysis. Who are the key stakeholders and what is the problem with each?
questions.guidance: Strong answers identify three stakeholder groups and their issues: (1) Insurance companies — already well-covered; drug is on most formularies; further outreach is saturated and not a lever. (2) Doctors/physicians — they are aware of the drug but have three specific misconceptions or gaps: they think it is very expensive, they do not believe it is on formularies (incorrect), and they are unsure when and to whom to prescribe it. This is the primary bottleneck. (3) Patients — low awareness and low engagement; they do not seek out specific blood pressure drugs from their doctors. Secondary lever but with upside through demand generation.

questions.prompt: Phase 3: Marketing ideas. What marketing initiatives would you recommend?
questions.guidance: Candidates should rule out insurance companies as a channel (already saturated). Focus should be on: DOCTORS — high-touch sales force visits to physician offices; materials clarifying formulary availability and correcting the cost misconception; clinical guidelines on appropriate patient segments (e.g., patients with adherence issues or those at high risk from missed doses). PATIENTS — direct-to-consumer advertising highlighting the missed-dose safety benefit; messaging must be balanced to avoid encouraging reckless behavior (moral hazard); goal is to create pull demand where patients proactively ask their doctor for this specific drug, potentially making it the first 'celebrity' blood pressure drug.

brainstorming.prompt: What marketing initiatives could increase sales of the drug among doctors and patients?

categories.name: Physician-focused initiatives
ideas: High-touch sales force visits to physician offices to build awareness
Educational materials clarifying that the drug is on formularies and correcting cost misconceptions
Clinical prescribing guidelines identifying the right patient segments (e.g., adherence-challenged patients)
KOL (key opinion leader) engagement to endorse appropriate use cases
CME (continuing medical education) programs featuring the drug's clinical profile

categories.name: Patient-focused initiatives
ideas: Direct-to-consumer TV or digital advertising highlighting the missed-dose safety benefit
Balanced messaging to avoid moral hazard (patients should not deliberately skip doses)
Campaign encouraging patients to ask their doctors for this specific drug by name
Patient support programs or co-pay assistance to reduce sticker shock at $25/month vs. $4 generic
Disease awareness campaigns on hypertension risks to prime the market

recommendation: The root cause of dismal sales is an information and education gap at the physician level — doctors incorrectly believe the drug is expensive and not covered by insurance, and lack guidance on when to prescribe it; this must be addressed first through targeted high-touch sales and educational materials

Secondary opportunity: launch a direct-to-consumer campaign around the drug's unique missed-dose safety benefit to create patient pull demand, potentially establishing it as the leading branded hypertension drug before all ARP competitors go fully generic within two years
risks: Physicians may remain skeptical of value vs. $4 generics even after education — need a strong clinical narrative
DTC campaigns could create moral hazard if patients interpret them as permission to skip doses
ARP going fully generic within two years removes the price-parity reference point, making $25 copay stand out more against $4 generics
Low end of efficacy range (14 mmHg vs. up to 17 mmHg) may limit uptake among physicians who prioritize maximum blood pressure reduction
next_steps: Deploy sales force for high-touch physician office visits with formulary and cost clarification materials within 30 days
Develop prescribing decision aids identifying target patient profiles (e.g., patients with known adherence challenges)
Design and test a DTC advertising concept focused on the missed-dose safety benefit with balanced risk messaging
Monitor prescription volume by physician segment to assess impact of sales force efforts over 90 days
